new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Copies checked (our source list 'held' is empty but the directory exists with 21 files +). (1) Easterday 2019 LSP PDF: extracted text of PDF p.395 shows '[dow] Doyayo / Atlantic-Congo, Volta-Congo (Cameroon) / References consulted: Wiering & Wiering (1994)' with printed page number 379; PDF p.396 lines 14-16 read exactly 'Suprasegmentals / Tone: Yes / Word stress: Not reported', printed page 380. Verbatim as quoted, locator correct. (2) sec. 8.1 p.1 reads verbatim: 'The description here, based on Marinus and Elisabeth Wiering (1994), is of the Poli dialect.. Every syllable carries one tone or a sequence of tones, which are indicated by means of raised numerals: 1 high, 2 mid-high, 3 mid-low…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Doyayo is described as a four-level tone language (every syllable bears a tone or tone sequence; roots monosyllabic, grammatical tone realised on the verb-root 'nuclear' syllable); the primary phonological description (Wiering & Wiering 1994, and by all indications its 1976 French precursor) makes no statement about word stress or accent, and no secondary source assigns Doyayo a stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None. The only position-sensitive facts reported are segmental: implosives and labiovelar stops are restricted to root-initial syllables (Beckman 1998: 55 after Wiering & Wiering 1994), and long vowels shorten before heavy coda clusters (Easterday 2019: 222 after W&W 1994: 22) -- neither is framed as stress.
new_statements.domain_note: All descriptions concern the Poli (Teere) dialect; statements are about lexical/grammatical tone on the word; no phrase-level accent discussed in accessible material.
new_statements.identity_note: All descriptive work (Wiering & Wiering 1974/1976/1994, Hewson n.d., Djataou 2012) is on the Poli variety of the Tɛ̰ɛ̰rɛ dialect of Doyayo (doya1240, ISO dow); other dialects are Markɛ (= 'Sewe' of older sources) and mountain Tɛ̰ɛ̰rɛ (Kleinewillinghoefer 2015). Jude 2012 may describe the mountain Tɛ̰ɛ̰rɛ variety. Language also appears as Doayo/Dowayo/Doowaayo/Namchi/Namshi.
